anomaly_def.Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging pipeline—covering in-memory log buffers, log file groups, flushing, switching, archiving, and replication retention—cannot keep pace with commit generation, making the log subsystem the primary bottleneck on the write path.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : One or more storage areas (data, log, archive, temp, backup, diagnostic) reach or approach physical or logical space exhaustion, causing allocation failures and stalling operations that require additional space.

When both anomalies are active, the database experiences compounding symptoms: commit latency and log-flush waits rise while free space in the online redo or archive destinations simultaneously plummets; log switches become abnormally frequent yet stall because the next log segment cannot be created; archiver or replication processes back up, filling remaining disk quickly; checkpoints and background writers thrash to reclaim space; DML sessions encounter "cannot allocate log", "out of space", or "archive destination full" errors; temporary-space and data-file growth operations may also fail, leading to widespread transaction timeouts, lock contention, and potential instance-wide freeze.

Causally, an overloaded log subsystem emits log data faster than it can be flushed or archived, accelerating space consumption in the log and archive areas. As space dwindles, the storage capacity anomaly prevents new log segments or archives from being created, which in turn blocks log switches and commit processing, amplifying log-write latency. The stalled log pipeline then prolongs transaction hold times, increases in-memory pressure, and may force emergency checkpoints that further inflate I/O and space demand. Thus each root cause feeds the other: slow or stuck log handling hastens space exhaustion, while space exhaustion further degrades log throughput, spiraling the database into a hard stop unless both logging performance and free-space availability are simultaneously remediated.

entry.official_description: Cannot close file %s, because it is in use
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with file creation, filesystem access, write durability, log persistence, tablespace management, or storage-capacity boundaries.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect filesystem capacity and permissions, verify persistence paths, review log and data placement, and check whether storage latency or write failures are affecting the engine.
